comments.text:
Comparing TAA performance to DLSS performance is basically pointless as TAA costs barely anything per frame. You might as well compare against No AA.

 DLSS is only gaining performance because it is rendering at roughly 67% deficit per axis and using an AI driven temporal upsample.
 DLSS is nice, don't get me wrong, but it fails in several key areas when it comes to Anti Aliaising, in areas that TAA doesn't (which is often terrible quality anyway. Like FFXVs garbage TAA, and in UE4 TAA. ). So it is disappointing from a quality stand point, but a nice alternative at least to TAA that has the bonus of not having many artifacts TAA introduces and only failing at actual AA issues. Rather than introducing artifacts and being poor quality.

DLSS shows the most issues in the UE4 demo thanks the massive aliasing generated by the engine's very harsh rendering. UE4 TAA is a smudged mess of ugliness to compensate. Hence why DLSS doesn't fare as well at a glance compared to TAA, but really just shows the weakness of the ability to really properly resolve worst case scenarios of an engine with extreme aliasing.


DlSS will be limited by limited game integration and Ray tracing will be useless. Bad performance and tons of visual artifacts introduced by it and by temporal filtering trying to clean up the low sample Ray tracing.

DLSS is practically bogus. Hardware Unboxed ran a detailed analysis and concluded that the end result looks comparable to just rendering the frame in 1800p and scaling it up to 4k normally. All that DLSS brings to the table, is a dedicated part of silicon for doing so, which increases overall performance a bit by taking some load off the CUDA cores. But it also needs complex preparations, running the game through nVidia's supercomputer first, and then sending specific mini drivers to the customers, so it will only ever work for a subset of games. If nVidia had just added dedicated silicon for regular AA, or even just more CUDA cores, the performance improvements would have been in the same ballpark - with a much less complicated procedure to even make use of them.

Why would anyone spend extra money on an unnecessarily complicated device whose effect you can achieve by simply rendering the games in 1800p? It makes no sense, just like the rest of the 20 series.

I need to replace my old and failing GTX 970, and had set money aside to go full in this time. But this new generation is so disappointing in so many ways (performance, power draw, temperature under long and heavy load, price, gimmick features instead of real improvements ...), I'll just buy a cheap 1060 6G and wait with my "big" upgrade until the next gen. Yeah, it's BS. And people claiming "well obviously it'll be more expensive because it's more powerful!" um...that's now how this is supposed to work. After years of tech developments & prices coming down, the new gen that replaces the previous one is supposed to release for around the same price as the card it's replacing!

Same with consoles. The PS4 came out 7 years after the PS3, yet it was $100-$200 LESS expensive. Consoles always hovered around $200-$300 at launch until we hit the HD era, then they hovered around $300-$400 at launch (with the PS3 exception). Then later in their lifecycles, they come down to $200-$300, putting them in line with traditional console prices. 

They don't keep going up & up & up because "they're more powerful." They're replacing the prior tech, and now expected to fit in that price range. Nvidia is trying to gouge the customer & pretend we aren't aware of that. I'm not buying a new card until the prices come down, or AMD releases a card that's comparable in power for a better price. I haven't bought one of their cards in over a decade, but now I regret it...as Nvidia has a virtual monopoly over the high-end GPU industry.
